Token-Based Communities & NFTs in Practice - assigned reading

questions.question_stem: A museum issues NFTs that it says represent ownership of physical artworks. Which analysis best respects the on-chain/off-chain boundary?
questions.correct_answer: Ethereum can record token ownership and transfers, but legal ownership of the physical artwork depends on off-chain agreements and institutions.
incorrect_answers: Ethereum can transfer the artwork's legal title when the NFT moves, but later custody disputes still depend on gallery records and court filings.
Ethereum can verify the museum's provenance claims from token history, while courts handle forged documents and custodial disputes across institutions.
Ethereum can bind each token to the current physical possessor of the artwork, while appraisers and insurers determine off-chain value during later disputes.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames tokens as programmable claims on a shared ledger. The chain can enforce ownership of the token and contract state, but the meaning attached to that token requires off-chain legal, social, or institutional support.

questions.question_stem: A game wants one contract to manage a fungible in-game currency, many identical consumable items, and several unique character skins. Which standard best fits that design pressure?
questions.correct_answer: ERC-1155, because it tracks balances by both address and token ID and can support multiple fungible or non-fungible item types.
incorrect_answers: ERC-20, because one fungible balance can represent currency, consumables, and skins if item categories are tracked in metadata too.
ERC-721, because unique token IDs can represent every currency unit, consumable, and skin inside one collection contract with metadata.
Separate ERC-20 and ERC-721 contracts, because wallet compatibility requires each item category to use its own token standard for support.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats standards as architectural commitments. ERC-1155 is suited to multi-token systems because balances are tracked per address and ID pair, unlike ERC-20's fungible balances or ERC-721's one-owner-per-token-ID model.

questions.question_stem: Why is choosing a token standard not merely a cosmetic implementation detail?
questions.correct_answer: The standard affects transfer granularity, identity model, wallet support, marketplace compatibility, indexer behavior, and future application logic.
incorrect_answers: The standard mainly fixes validator fee markets, transaction ordering, wallet connection flows, and how quickly transfers confirm on-chain.
The standard mainly establishes copyright terms, custody duties, tax treatment, and venue rules for off-chain asset disputes after resale.
The standard mainly chooses the compiler, storage database, node networking format, and consensus checks used during contract execution.
questions.explanation: ERC standards coordinate technical and social expectations across contracts, wallets, markets, and indexers. That coordination shapes what later applications can safely assume about the token.

questions.question_stem: An NFT's `tokenURI` points to an ordinary HTTP URL controlled by the issuer. What is the main integrity concern?
questions.correct_answer: The token can remain on-chain while the metadata or media at that location changes, disappears, or becomes misleading.
incorrect_answers: The token becomes invalid when the URL server is down because ownership is stored in the issuer's database instead of Ethereum.
The token history becomes harder for indexers to read because HTTP metadata replaces events emitted by the NFT contract.
The image is embedded in the owner's wallet, so each transfer must rewrite the media file for the next address.
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes token permanence from metadata integrity. A location-addressed URL depends on a mutable server location, while content addressing provides stronger evidence that the referenced content has not changed.

questions.question_stem: A token-gated Discord checks wallet ownership before letting users enter a channel. What does the token gate actually enforce in this setup?
questions.correct_answer: It can condition access on current wallet ownership, while moderation, culture, server availability, and content hosting remain off-chain systems.
incorrect_answers: It can make Discord's chat server decentralized, while the token contract still handles ownership checks and role assignment for each channel itself.
It can verify that each wallet maps to one real participant, while Discord operators still manage moderation, roles, and account bans across accounts.
It can enforce binding governance participation, while proposal review, voting snapshots, and treasury execution stay socially managed after admission.
questions.explanation: The lesson presents token communities as two-layer systems. The ownership check may be on-chain or wallet-based, but the community experience usually depends on social and operational infrastructure outside Ethereum.

questions.question_stem: A project uses an NFT as a membership badge and a fungible token to vote on treasury spending. How should a student classify this design?
questions.correct_answer: It is a hybrid token-community design where access or identity and governance power are handled by different token patterns.
incorrect_answers: It is a pure DAO design because the fungible token handles votes while the NFT only records profile status for roles.
It is only a membership NFT design, because the badge determines admission even if another token governs treasury voting rights.
It is a social-token model where one fungible community asset controls identity, access, and treasury decisions.
questions.explanation: The lesson treats DAOs, membership NFTs, and social tokens as patterns that can be combined. The important question is what each token controls, not which brand label the community uses.

questions.question_stem: A public mint lets anyone call `mint()` until the supply cap is reached. Why should minting be treated as a distribution-policy decision, not just token creation?
questions.correct_answer: The mint logic decides initial ownership and can shape scarcity, fairness, bot exposure, payments, allowlists, signatures, and operator power.
incorrect_answers: The mint only publishes collection metadata and leaves ownership, supply, transfer limits, and payment rules to marketplace settings.
The mint is mostly a wallet-display step, since validator selection decides scarcity, sale order, allowlists, and bot exposure rules.
The token standard fixes the mint price and cap, so the project team mainly chooses art files and marketplace listings after launch.
questions.explanation: Minting is a state-writing transaction that creates a token ID or balance and assigns an initial owner. Contract rules at that moment encode economic and governance choices.
questions.specific_source_lesson: /tmp/blockchain-course-slide-only/ethereum_06-EF-token_based_communities_and_nfts_in_practice-slides-only.qmd: What Is Minting? / Minting on Ethereum / Minting And Distribution Policy

questions.question_stem: A marketplace reads an NFT royalty field but chooses not to pay royalties on resale. Which conclusion best describes what is happening?
questions.correct_answer: Royalty metadata can signal creator payment expectations, but payment may still depend on marketplace enforcement and surrounding off-chain norms.
incorrect_answers: Ethereum consensus enforces royalty payment after each resale, so nonpayment means the resale should be treated as invalid by wallets.
A royalty field transfers copyright license terms to the buyer, while resale payments are handled through ordinary gas accounting rules.
Creators can recover unpaid royalties by reversing secondary transfers through the same standard field marketplaces read without marketplace cooperation.
questions.explanation: The lesson uses royalty signaling to reinforce the enforced-versus-signaled distinction. A standard can communicate expectations to marketplaces without guaranteeing every downstream venue enforces them.

questions.question_stem: In the DAO re-entrancy case, why did the exploit work even though Ethereum consensus and cryptography were functioning?
questions.correct_answer: The contract sent ETH before updating internal balances, allowing recursive withdrawals before the state reflected the first withdrawal.
incorrect_answers: The contract checked balances only after an oracle updated prices, letting the attacker borrow against a stale token valuation.
The caller's fallback function ran during the ETH send, but the contract had already reduced the withdrawable balance first.
The hard fork changed the contract's bytecode during withdrawal, letting recursive calls bypass the DAO's original accounting before the fork vote.
questions.explanation: The lesson frames the DAO attack as a smart-contract sequencing failure. The chain faithfully executed vulnerable logic; checks-effects-interactions is one way to avoid that ordering bug.

questions.question_stem: A dApp stops working for most users because its main RPC provider has an outage, but Ethereum L1 continues producing blocks. What concept does this illustrate?
questions.correct_answer: Decentralized base-layer consensus can coexist with centralized operational chokepoints in RPC access, bridges, or oracles.
incorrect_answers: ERC token standards define RPC failover behavior first, so NFT-heavy apps lose access until metadata servers resync.
L1 consensus pauses whenever a popular provider fails to relay user transactions through its hosted endpoint for most wallets.
Bridges and oracles inherit Ethereum consensus security directly, so their outages imply a base-chain fork later.
questions.explanation: The lesson closes by separating Ethereum L1 from service layers built above it. Analysts should evaluate concentrated infrastructure dependencies even when the base chain remains healthy.

questions.question_stem: How could soulbound tokens improve NFT provenance without proving off-chain truth by themselves?
questions.correct_answer: They can attach works to an issuing Soul's reputation, affiliations, and prior attestations, giving buyers social context to evaluate authenticity.
incorrect_answers: They can make the artist's legal identity visible in every wallet, giving buyers strong assurance that copied media is unauthorized online.
They can move collection metadata on-chain, giving buyers technical proof that creator claims and institution records are accurate for resale.
They can replace issuer credibility with transfer limits, making every credential attached to a Soul trustworthy by default for community use.
questions.explanation: The reading's claim is narrower than automatic truth. SBTs can add verifiable social context and issuer reputation, but credibility, revocation, and off-chain interpretation still matter.

questions.question_stem: Two DAO votes have the same number of supporting wallets. In one vote, most supporters share the same issuer attestations and affiliations; in the other, supporters come from socially distant communities. What mechanism addresses this difference?
questions.correct_answer: Correlation-aware governance can discount highly correlated Souls because shared SBT patterns may indicate sybils, collusion, common bias, or over-coordination.
incorrect_answers: One-token-one-vote governance can handle the disparity by treating larger balance holders as better proxies for independent social groups in both votes.
Souldrops address the issue by granting extra voting weight to people with the same affiliations because they form clearer communities without additional evidence.
Standard Nakamoto coefficients can determine social distance because address counts already capture independence across communities and affiliations.
questions.explanation: The reading argues that decentralization cannot be measured only by wallet counts or token balances. Shared SBTs can reveal correlation, and governance can try to reward cooperation across social distance.
questions.specific_source_reading: /tmp/blockchain-course-readings/text/desoc.txt: DAO Governance And Decentralization / Correlation discounting

questions.question_stem: A platform proposes making all education, employment, and membership SBTs public so anyone can verify credentials. What is the strongest concern with this approach?
questions.correct_answer: Public credentials can aid verification, but they can also expose sensitive affiliations and enable discrimination, coercive access controls, or social-credit dynamics.
incorrect_answers: Public SBTs would make eligibility checks easier, but privacy concerns would be limited to hiding profile pages from casual viewers across schools and employers.
Keeping attestations private would resolve the issue, because governance can verify credentials and social distance without disclosure tradeoffs in every governance setting.
Non-transferability mainly creates a resale-market problem, while discrimination risk comes from issuer behavior rather than public visibility for users.
questions.explanation: The reading treats privacy and publicity as a structural tradeoff. Some visibility supports provenance and sybil resistance, but too much visibility can turn social trust infrastructure into surveillance and exclusion infrastructure.
